title: The Light That Looked Down
excerpt: Before the morning star fell, he came down to look at a man - and saw himself.
body:
Before the morning star fell, he came down to look at a man - and saw himself.

Reader, imagine a man - he stands at the edge of the garden as the day retires, the air has no fault in it, the grass beneath his feet has never met a thorn. He has no past to mourn, no grief to live in the shadow of, only the present - and the present is enough for him. Not for long.

Above him there is a light. Not the sun, the sun has gone down - this light does not go down. It moves as a man moves, it walks the ridge of the evening as a general walks the ridge before the armies have assembled. It is the bearer of light, the morning star, the most beautiful of all things God has made - and he has not yet fallen.

He has come down to look at the man.

"So this is him" the light says - not to the man, to himself.

The man looks up. He is not afraid, fear has not yet been born into the world. "Who are you ?"

"I carry the light before the dawn. I was there when the foundations were laid, I sang when the stars were hung in their places. I have come to see what all of heaven is talking about."

"And what is heaven talking about ?"

"You."

Notice: the first wound is not a lie - it is attention.

The man had never been the subject of anything. He named the animals, he tended the garden, he walked with God in the cool of the day - content as a child is content, naive, a shade from the garden before the fall. Now a being of fire tells him heaven speaks his name, and for the first time in all his days the man thinks about the man.

The light sits beside him on the ridge. He does not sit as a servant sits - he sits as a prince sits beside a peasant he has found interesting.

"Tell me what you do" he says.

"I tend what is given to me. I name what is brought to me. I walk with Him."

"And when He is not here ?"

"He is always here."

The light smiles - the most beautiful smile the man has ever seen, he has nothing to compare it to and yet he knows. "Is He ? Then why does He walk with you only in the cool of the day ? Where is He in the heat ?"

The man has no answer, he has never needed one. One thought enters - one thousand march behind it.

*

But Reader, do not think the light is merely the tempter here, look closer. He has not fallen, he does not yet know what he will become. He came down because he was curious, and curiosity is a hunger for the unknown - we desire the unknown, we hate when it is granted.

He looks at the man and sees a thing made of dust that God loves. He looks at himself and sees a thing made of fire that God also loves - but differently ? less ? He cannot tell. He extrapolates, and if I extrapolate all I see, have I really seen anything ?

"Do you know what I am ?" the light asks.

"Beautiful."

"Yes." He says it too quickly - he hears himself say it. A small thing, a trifle, yet the halls of heaven are so quiet a trifle echoes in them for an age.

*

He returns the next night, and the next. Every night the light comes down the ridge, and every night the man waits for it - he waits, hoping one will find him, and one does.

They talk. The light teaches him the names of the stars, the man had only ever called them lights. He teaches him that a thought can be turned over and examined, that you can look at a thing and then look at yourself looking at the thing. Before, the man walked in the garden - now he watches himself walk in the garden. Self consciousness, the first hindrance, the first chain that looks like a bracelet.

"You see" the light says, "you are more than a gardener, you are a mind. The body is temporary, the mind is forever."

The man repeats it in the morning, alone, to the trees. It sounds wise. It sounds like his own.

And the light, flying back up through the fields of heaven, repeats something to himself too - he who once only sang now speaks, and he speaks from high but only a whisper he produces, the wind carries his sound though no one hears it. Nature looks at him, he looks at himself.

*

One night the man asks a question of his own.

"Do you ever wish to be Him ?"

The light goes still. The wind stops. Somewhere in the garden a bird stops in the middle of its song.

"Why would you ask that ?"

"Because you speak of Him the way I have begun to speak of you."

And here, Reader, is the true moment - not the serpent, not the fruit, not the war of swords and fire. The moment is a question from a creature of dust, and the light looks into it as into a well polished mirror, and sees what he has been carrying the whole time without naming it.

He came to look at the man. He has been looking at himself.

"I was the first light" he says slowly. "Before the sun, before you. I was the one who held it up so the rest could see - was it not me ? Who carried it ? Who stood closest ? And He takes dirt and breathes into it and gives it a garden and walks with it - and I am to bow ?"

The man says nothing. He recognises the voice. It is his own voice, from the mornings, speaking to the trees.

"Adequacy" the light says, "is the enemy of those who strive for greatness."

"Is it ?" the man asks.

"Is it not ?"

And neither of them knows anymore who taught whom.

*

"I will tell you a secret" the light says, "and you will keep it for me. There is nothing you cannot do - nothing. He tells you there are limits because limits keep you small. Pride is only the name the small give to the great."

The original lie - you can do whatever you want. Notice: he did not tell it to the man first. He told it to himself, the man was merely in the room.

The man lies awake that night. He holds one thing in his left hand, another in his right. In the left the garden, the cool of the day, the walking, the being known. In the right the light, the mind, the stars with their names, the feeling of being spoken of in heaven. He knows he can only hold one at a time. Tears are in his eyes - he does not yet know what tears are for.

*

What happened after is written elsewhere, by other hands - the war, the third of the stars swept down, the lightning falling from the heights. Reader, those are the drums of war, and the battle cries are only the foreshadowing of the screams and clanks of Hades. I am not interested in the war. I am interested in the night before it.

The night before, the light came down the ridge one last time. He did not walk like a general now. He walked like a man - and that is the most terrible thing I can tell you.

"I am going to ask Him" he said. "Tomorrow. I will stand before the throne and ask Him why."

"And if He answers ?"

"Then I will have my answer."

"And if He does not ?"

The light looked out over the garden, so beautiful, without fault - and for a moment the man saw something pass over the face of the most beautiful thing ever made. Not anger. Grief. The grief of one who already knows what he is about to destroy, and will destroy it anyway, because he has convinced himself he is infallible - because he has already made up his mind.

"Then I will build my own heaven" he said. "Out of whatever is left."

The man wanted to ask him - can one sleep in hell ? But he did not. He had learned, from the light, that some questions are better kept.

*

In the morning the sky was the same. That is what no one tells you - the sky was the same. The sun rose, the garden breathed, the animals carried their names. But the ridge was empty, and it stayed empty.

The man waited. He waited, hoping one would find him - no one came.

What he did not understand, what he would not understand until the fruit was in his mouth and the cool of the day became a thing to hide from, is that the light had not left. It had only stopped being outside of him.

It sat now in the halls of his mind, conversing among his thoughts. It said: you have been awake long enough, rest. It said: only you could think these things. It said: maybe if you sin in private He won't see. It was never loud. Gossip is never explicit - words of war are whispered esoterically.

*

Reader, you were told the devil fell because he wanted to be God. Perhaps. I think he fell because he looked down at something beneath him and saw himself in it, and could not bear what he saw - so he called it greatness and walked into the fire, telling himself it was the light.

He subjected himself to hell willingly; he only told himself it was glory he was walking into.

And the man ? The man did what men do. He built a fortress of his mind and called it wisdom, he retreated into it like an army routing from battle, and he sealed the cave shut. He lived in the shadow of a grief he could not name - grief for a friend who was never his friend, for a light that was only ever a mirror.

Every night he looked up at the stars. He knew all of their names now. He searched for the brightest one, the one that rose before the dawn.

It was never there.

What force could redeem such a man - surely not himself.

title: The Watchman on the Wall
excerpt: A man guards a city from everything except the one thing he cannot stop watching.
body:
A man guards a city from everything except the one thing he cannot stop watching.

Reader, imagine a man - he stands on the wall of a city that no longer has enemies. The wars were won long ago, the gates have rusted open, the trumpets hang silent in the armoury, yet every evening he climbs the stair and takes his post. No one has ordered him to. He has ordered himself. A man must guard something, he says - and if there is no enemy outside, he will find one within.

Below the wall runs a path to the well. At the hour the sun leans on the rooftops, a girl walks it with a jar on her shoulder. She does not look up. Why would she ? Walls are not looked at - they are only walked beside.

He looks down.

*

The first evening it was nothing - a figure on a path, a jar, a shadow lengthening. The second evening he noticed the jar was blue. The third, he noticed she walked faster going down than coming back, as if the water were heavier than the emptiness. By the tenth evening he knew the sound her sandals made on the third stone, which was loose, and he waited for it the way a priest waits for the bell.

Notice: he did not decide to watch her. He decided only to keep his post. The watching arrived on its own, as all slaveries do - quietly, dressed as a duty.

He tells himself he is guarding the city. He is guarding a path.

*

He never learns her name. He gives her one, then takes it back, for a name personifies a thing, and he does not wish her to become a person - a person can refuse you. A figure on a path cannot.

So he builds her. From the jar, from the hour, from the way she pauses at the bend to shift the weight - he builds a woman. He gives her a mind that reads what he reads. He gives her a sorrow that mirrors his own. He gives her a reason for never looking up, and the reason is always him: she knows he is there, she is too proud, too shy, too wise, she is waiting for him to descend.

He is the architect of a city of one, and he has made her its only citizen.

*

Reader, you will ask - why does he not simply come down ? The stair is right there. Forty steps, the old soldiers counted, worn smooth in the middle by a century of boots. He could take them in a minute. He could stand by the well when she comes and say anything - good evening, the water is cold, your jar is a beautiful colour. Any word would do. Any word would break the spell, which is precisely why he does not say one.

On the wall he is a watchman. On the path he would be a man - and a man can be seen, and weighed, and found wanting.

He calls it honour - a man of my station does not chase water-girls down a stair. He calls it patience - all things happen in providence, if it is meant she will look up. He calls it wisdom, he calls it restraint, he calls it the discipline of the old philosophers, and he has a hundred names for it, and not one of them is its true name, which is fear.

*

In the night the devil climbs the stair. He is not a beast, he has no horns - he is an old comrade from the wars, and he leans on the parapet beside the watchman like a friend.

"She looked up today" the devil says. "Did you not see ? At the bend, the smallest glance."

The watchman did not see it. He has been watching for a hundred evenings and never once seen it. But now, having been told, he remembers it - he remembers it vividly - a tilt of the head, a flicker of attention, meant for him.

"Go down tomorrow" the devil says. "She is waiting."

And the watchman lies awake with the glance that never happened, polishing it like a medal.

The next night the devil comes again, and this time his voice is cold. "She has never looked up. She does not know you exist. To her you are a stone in the wall - and who would love a stone ?" And the watchman, who an hour ago was a lover, is now a fool, and the shame of it burns the back of his neck.

Reader, notice the trick - both voices kept him on the wall. Hope said wait, she is coming. Despair said wait, there is no point. Neither one said: go down.

*

Seasons turn on the city. The figs ripen and drop and are trodden into the path. He learns the girl by the weather - in the heat she walks slowly, in the rain she runs, and once in winter she slips at the third stone and his whole body leans over the parapet as if he could catch her from forty steps above. She rises, brushes her knee, gathers the jar. She did not need him. She never needed him.

He writes that night - for he writes, the watchman, by a small lamp in the guardhouse, aphorisms no one will read. He writes: it is true imprisonment to love what you will not approach. He reads it back and feels wise. Then he climbs the stair again at dawn to see if she has come early.

Knowledge has never once saved him. A man can describe his chains perfectly and still wear them.

*

He begins to pray about her. Not for her - about her. He kneels in the guardhouse facing the east, and in the place where the icon is, her shape arrives - the jar, the bend, the blue. He tries to put God back in that place, and the shape returns, patient as water. He has built an idol without lifting a chisel. He has made a god of a girl who has never once looked at him, and he bows to it twice a day, at the hour she goes down and the hour she comes back.

What a strange religion - its god does not know she is one, and its only worshipper keeps the temple locked from the inside.

*

One night he dreams he has come down. The forty steps pass under him like nothing, the path is warm, the well is deep and black and smells of old stone. She is there, the blue jar resting on the lip of the well, and he speaks - he cannot hear what he says, only that it is perfect, that it is everything he has composed on the wall for a year. And she turns to him.

Her face is not the face he built. It is plainer, and stranger, and tired about the eyes. She does not read what he reads. She does not carry his sorrow. She looks at him the way one looks at a stranger who has spoken too warmly - politely, waiting for him to finish, already turning back to the water.

He wakes before dawn with his heart beating like the drums of war. And here is the darkest thing, Reader - he is relieved. Relieved it was only a dream. Relieved she is still up there in his mind, unspoiled - the blue jar, the bend, the glance that never happened. He would rather keep the woman he made than meet the one who exists.

He climbs the stair and takes his post, and when she passes beneath him at the hour, he loves her more than ever - for now he knows what it would cost to be wrong.

*

Then one evening the path is empty.

The sun leans on the rooftops at the proper hour. The third stone waits, loose, for its sound. Nothing. He tells himself she is sick, delayed, the well is crowded. The next evening, nothing. On the seventh evening another girl walks the path with a red jar, laughing with a friend, and she is nobody.

He never learns what happened. Perhaps she married. Perhaps her family moved to another quarter, another city, another country across the sea. Perhaps she simply found a nearer well. It does not matter. What matters is that she had a life, a whole life, with rooms and voices and mornings he would never see - and in all of it, he had been nothing. Not a lost chance, not a regret, not a name half remembered. Nothing. A wall she walked beside.

She will never know she was watched. She will never know she was worshipped. She will never know that for a year a man stood above her each evening and built a city in her honour, and let no one into it - least of all her.

*

He keeps his post. What else is there ? The wall is still there and so is he. He climbs the forty steps each evening, looks down on an empty path, and tells himself he is guarding the city.

Sometimes, near the hour, he hears a sandal on the third stone and his heart leaps like an animal in a trap. It is never her. It is the wind, or a child, or the stone settling on its own.

He has learned one thing, and he wrote it down: the watchman who will not leave the wall is not guarding the city - he is its prisoner, the wall is his cell, and he holds the only key.

Reader, I would like to tell you that he came down at last. That one evening he took the forty steps, walked the path himself, drew water from the well, felt how heavy the jar was, and understood her.

But you know him. You have stood on walls of your own. The heart is haughty - it believes it can wait out fate.

The path is empty. The jar is gone. And still, at the hour, the watchman leans over the parapet, looking down at nothing, waiting for someone to look up.

title: Pride Begins With I
excerpt: At times it can feel as if my God has left me; at others I am aware of the reality that I left Him.
body:
At times it can feel as if my God has left me; at others I am aware of the reality that I left Him.

Pride begins with "I", not with God.

You boasted of your works; you only riled up the enemy, not yourself.

How much time did you spend boasting? How much time did you spend thanking Him who created you?

You let anger stir you up, you allow hatred to steer you against the winds - have you forgotten who commands the winds? He Himself, the logos.

Even if you built an empire, you yourself would still be a sick man.

title: Closing Preamble: Manuscript
body:
I finish reading.

The philosopher stands beside the window, his eyes directed towards the world outside.

He turns.

“Have you found what you sought?”

“No.”

“Then what have you found?”

I consider the question.

A man who desires, yet wishes to appear indifferent. A man who proclaims the rule of reason, yet permits his passions to determine which objects reason must investigate.

A man who wants to be approached, yet retreats from the very person whose approach he desires.

Alas, what a pitiful contradiction.

The philosopher approaches the desk.

“Do you still believe the figure possesses some hidden meaning?”

“Perhaps.”

“And what if it does not?”

“Then I have wasted my time.”

“And if it does?”

“Then I have failed to discover it.”

“Must these be the only possibilities?”

I remember the warnings of my own conscience - do not fall into false dichotomies.

Yet here I am, having constructed another.

I tell him, “There was once a time when the woman smiled upon seeing me, when words passed between us without difficulty, when her presence was an ordinary part of my day. Now I find myself avoiding her eyes, measuring my conduct, wondering whether to speak or remain silent. Surely something has changed?”

“Something has changed,” he replies.

“Then you acknowledge it?”

“Yes.”

“What has changed?”

“Tell me.”

I become irritated.

“Must I provide every answer myself? You were among the greatest philosophers of your civilisation, yet you stand before me asking questions which I have spent weeks attempting to answer!”

He remains silent.

Then he asks, “Have you considered that the change which troubles you may not exist entirely within her?”

I look away.

The heart becomes agitated.

It desires to defend itself, to bring forth its evidence, to establish once and for all that the events were not imagined.

Yet the mind begins to consider another possibility.

What if I have altered the very conditions by which I observe her?

What if my attempts to conceal my desires have made me appear indifferent?

What if the apparent distance between us is not entirely a distance she has created?

Alas, the man who hides his thoughts from another then laments that they remain unknown.

But what if she truly is indifferent?

Then let her be indifferent.

What authority have I over the will of another? I may govern my own conduct, my words and the direction of my actions, yet I cannot command the thoughts of a woman who possesses a life entirely separate from mine.

The philosopher looks towards the triangle.

“Why do you require this figure to be completed?”

“Because I desire to know what it represents.”

“And if no conclusion can be reached?”

“Then I shall remain uncertain.”

“Would uncertainty destroy you?”

I consider this.

Perhaps not.

Yet what strange torment it is, to possess a mind which demands finality while living in a world which offers little of it.

The philosopher takes the manuscript.

“Young man, you have devoted yourself to the investigation of a woman, yet I suspect you are searching for something beyond her.”

“What might that be?”

“Ask yourself.”

I look towards the books upon my desk.

The philosopher who had spent his life examining the nature of knowledge now asks me to examine the very instrument with which I seek it.

How strange.

I tell him, “Perhaps I merely desire the restoration of what once existed.”

“And what existed?”

I hesitate.

A smile? Conversation? Companionship? The possibility of something greater?

Or perhaps merely the hope that another human being might recognise something within me which I have struggled to recognise within myself.

The philosopher remains silent.

I ask, “Is it not possible that providence brought us together?”

“It is possible.”

“Then perhaps there is some purpose to it?”

“Perhaps.”

“And if I never discover that purpose?”

“Would it cease to have existed?”

I cannot answer.

The philosopher approaches the doorway.

“Remember,” he says, “the world does not suspend its movements while one man attempts to understand them.”

With those words he departs.

I am alone.

The room returns to silence, the books remain in their former positions, the triangle lies before me.

Had he truly appeared?

Or had the mind, fatigued by its own reflections, constructed another world in which to continue its arguments?

Perhaps I have not spoken to the philosopher at all.

Perhaps I have merely allowed my own conscience to speak through the image of a man whose writings I hold in such high regard.

Alas, how cunning is the mind!

Even in the pursuit of truth it may create an illusion, then rebuke itself through the very illusion it has created.

I look towards the triangle once more.

What is the third point?

Is it the relationship between the two persons? Their positions within the physical world? The meaning attached to their movements?

Or is it the observer, the man who stands beyond the figure, imagining himself detached from the very thing which consumes him?

I cannot say.

I know what occurred before my eyes.

I know what I remember.

But what have I truly established?

The woman remains beyond my knowledge, living within her own world. Perhaps she remembers these events, perhaps they are trifles to her, perhaps what I regard as extraordinary has been entirely ordinary in her experience.

I cannot enter her conscience.

Yet I have spent so much time attempting to do so that I have neglected the government of my own.

What a strange reversal - the philosopher who sought to understand the world has become a slave to his interpretation of it.

I rise from the desk.

The lamp burns low.

I look towards the darkness outside.

Tomorrow the world will continue. The woman may smile, she may not. She may speak, she may remain silent. She may return to her former place, or perhaps that place has ceased to hold any significance to her.

I shall have to live regardless.

But have I truly accepted this?

Or have I merely written another argument in favour of a virtue which I have not yet acquired?

I extinguish the lamp.

The triangle remains.

And as I depart the chamber, one final question presents itself:

Have I been investigating the distance between myself and another, or has the greatest distance all along been that between the man I claim to be and the man who conducts himself before her?

Alas, perhaps the third point was never hers to provide.

title: Opening Preamble: Manuscript
excerpt: Reader, imagine a man - he sits before his desk, surrounded by the writings of men who have long since departed this earth, men whose bodies have returned to dust, yet whose thoughts continue to command the attention of the living.
body:
Reader, imagine a man - he sits before his desk, surrounded by the writings of men who have long since departed this earth, men whose bodies have returned to dust, yet whose thoughts continue to command the attention of the living.

Before him lie several pages, upon one he has drawn a triangle, points representing the positions of two people within a room.

How strange, that a man who has spent so much time investigating the greatest questions of existence should now find himself investigating the movement of a woman from one chair to another.

He looks at the figure.

He remembers her sitting beside him, he remembers her smile, the movement of her eyes, the conversations which followed. Yet what has happened since? The two who once sat beside one another now appear as strangers, each occupying their own world.

Alas, what has become of him?

He came to university seeking knowledge, yet finds himself investigating a woman whose thoughts remain completely unknown to him.

Surely this is foolishness?

But were his observations not real? Did these things not occur before his very eyes? Is he to deny reality merely because his interpretation of it causes him suffering?

He sits back, his thoughts begin conversing among themselves, each attempting to establish authority over the other.

Reason demands evidence.

Passion demands reassurance.

Pride refuses humiliation.

The conscience, having watched the entire affair unfold, asks whether any of these rulers have the interests of their master at heart.

One thought enters, a thousand march behind it - the mind has become an assembly of competing authorities, none willing to surrender its claim to truth.

He is fatigued.

He turns towards the writings of the ancients, believing that in their words he may find refuge from his own.

Yet what refuge is philosophy to the man who uses it to flee from reality?

He closes his eyes.

A figure appears before him, an elderly man, dressed in garments unfamiliar to the modern world. His face is stern, his appearance dignified, and his gaze that of one who has spent many years examining the follies of men.

He approaches the desk.

It is Plato.

The philosopher examines the books, the scattered pages and finally the triangular figure.

“What is this?” he asks.

“A representation of reality.”

“Of all reality?”

“No, of an observation.”

“And what have you observed?”

“The position of two persons, and the movement of one between places.”

“Then why have you drawn a figure which appears to concern more than their positions?”

I become agitated.

“Do you believe I have invented what occurred? I saw these things myself. The woman sat in one place, she gave her reason for moving, and she moved elsewhere. What fault can you find within the observation?”

“None,” he responds.

“Then what is your contention?”

“That you have mistaken the certainty of an event for the certainty of its meaning.”

Alas, how irritating is the philosopher who attacks an argument which has yet to be fully presented.

I rebuke him.

“Must we not use reason to extrapolate from the world around us? How else are we to understand the intentions of others?”

He looks towards the figure.

“Tell me, if the woman had remained seated, what would you have concluded?”

“That she was comfortable where she sat.”

“And because she moved?”

“That there may have been another reason.”

“May have been?”

“Yes.”

“Then why do you conduct yourself as though there certainly was?”

I remain silent.

The philosopher continues.

“You have constructed a world from what you know, and furnished the rest with what you suspect. You then enter this world, examine its contents, and call your conclusions knowledge.”

I look towards the triangle.

Perhaps he is correct.

Or perhaps I am merely yielding before the authority of a great philosopher, as the weaker man bends before one of greater reputation.

I ask him, “Are you saying that all human relations must remain unknowable?”

“Have I said that?”

“No.”

“Then why do you argue against it?”

Alas! Even in my defence of reason, my own reasoning appears to betray me.

The philosopher walks towards the bookshelf and withdraws a manuscript.

Its pages are worn, its contents unfamiliar.

“Here,” he says, “is the account of a man who sought to investigate another, yet in the course of his investigation became the very thing which required examination.”

I take the manuscript.

“Will this tell me what she thought?”

“No.”

“Will it tell me whether something existed between us?”

“No.”

“Then what purpose does it serve?”

He responds, “You have demanded knowledge of another while refusing to understand the disorder within yourself. Must every question lead you away from the man who asks it?”

I lower my eyes.

Upon the first page is written:

THE THIRD POINT

On the uncertainty of a woman, the pride of the heart, and the tyranny of interpretation.

title: Reflections: What Force Could Redeem Such a Man?
excerpt: He sits, looking upon the ruins of what once was, a commander of men, a conqueror of himself—or so he believed.
body:
He sits, looking upon the ruins of what once was, a commander of men, a conqueror of himself—or so he believed. Did the enemy breach his fortress, or had he willingly opened its gates? He cannot remember, though he claims to know the causes of his own destruction.

Reader, imagine a man—he holds one object in his left hand and another in his right. He sits up, staring at them, tears in his eyes. He knows he can only have one at a time. On the left, he holds his physical potential, his ability to dominate and command authority; on the right, he holds his greater, more natural gift: his intellect and ability to live among abstractions.

Virtue through reason, faith, and discipline.

Discipline is the master of greatness; endeavour, the teacher of hope.

Adequacy is the enemy of those who strive for greatness.

The breeze would hit you after a day of thorough use of your muscles; you would be covered in sweat and salt. You would walk around as an Olympian among men. What happened—how did that entity die?

Do you remember how strong you felt? You were a lion, ready to eat all who stood in your way. Did it die when she left, or did it die earlier, internally?

Don’t you remember? Any girl you wanted, you could get; anything you demanded, you could attain. And in the course of that length of time you know as the fall, you forgot yourself and betrayed all you called sacred.

The past is the window through which we view ourselves; we are merely shards of it, scattered parts of what once was.

Did you do something to warrant earthly damnation and humiliation? What made you fall from on high? Why can you not remember where you came from? Can’t you retrace the steps?

Stop! He screams to himself—how did I get here? This was meant to be my great moment? Now I look back on the ruins of what I once was?

It overwhelms him with a sudden bolt of thought—the grand revelation: he has fallen; the man he once was is no more.

Eating foods you said you would never eat, partaking in drinks you would’ve called disgraceful, spending too much time pondering on the dead, engaging in acts you never would’ve before—not only were you betrayed by that girl, but you betrayed yourself and all your values.

Lament is the light that illuminates my lampstand—from it I view the world.

This must surely cause death—living in the shadow of your own grief.

The army disintegrates, the commander looks upon his men, though no longer do they heed his orders. He orders them to stand, yet he himself retreats - the first act of betrayal coming not from the soldiers, but from the one who once commanded them.

What is left is a husk of a man, the man who ran from life. He fled like an army routed in battle—an army running into a cave and sealing it shut.

You were the commander of that army; your men died around you one by one. Before you knew it, you had forgotten your past life, war and conquest, victory and glory. You philosophised and abstracted yourself—you created your own world and forgot about the one you left behind.

The drums of war and the battle cries of the men who fight them are only the foreshadowing of the screams and clanks of Hades.

War is the risk that must be taken for fulfilment.

Don’t be hasty with the sword in battle; you can be struck back.

He enters the cave, believing he sees pleasure—it’s a trap. He is now forced to confront himself; he must investigate his desires—or are they not desires? He does not know—that is the torture of being trapped.

Within the cave he finds another kingdom, its inhabitants not men but thoughts, its battles not physical but metaphysical. He rejoices, believing himself free from the affairs of mortals, yet what has he conquered? He commands his thoughts, or do his thoughts command him?

Philosophy is where the men of the physical world run away from their problems; they run into the abyss of the metaphysical.

The words of the mind are more comfortable than the words of the physical.

He observes his days; he writes; the devil whispers in his ear—philosophy indeed.

He himself wants to be asked questions but hides from answers to his own. He speaks in riddles, a Gnosticism in which only he has the knowledge—knowledge of his own world.

He toils, yet he does not work; he labours, yet bears no fruit; he rests but is exercised—his life is hubris, living between the winds of life.

You let one thought in; one thousand thoughts march behind it, overriding your rationality.

Why does one thought lead to another? Can’t you pull yourself in?

Passion overwhelms reason, and reason introduces passion.

Hedonism is my master; pleasure, desire, degeneracy—whip me into submission. The woe of the primal man, the woe of him from whom virtue and discipline have fled.

My passions rage in me: paranoia, introversion, anxiety. At any moment, I feel I could spontaneously combust; at any moment, what did he mean by this or that? Is he out for me?

Don’t believe so. I genuinely do see myself as separate persons in one body. That part of me is a genuine other person who sneers at me. He is a dark figure; I look back at him with a blaze of suspicion.

The halls of the conscience become crowded, thoughts assemble as armies - each proclaiming itself the rightful ruler. He observes them, investigates them, yet never enters the battle; perhaps the commander has become a spectator to the destruction of his own kingdom.

The devil tells you, “You’ve been awake for five hours; don’t you think it’s time to rest?” He makes you focus on your past. Notice: he begs to blind you to your future.

The devil will twist good into bad. He says, “Go to the monastery, forget studying.” Notice: when you actually have time for the monastery with intention, he begs you not to.

The devil whispers in your ear, “Can’t you see? Only you have these thoughts and can write these things!” The enemy wants you to become fat with pride; when convenient, they will slaughter you like a pig.

You thought you could deceive God; He handed you over to your own foundations, faulty as they are. You fell through.

You ridicule yourself, investigating every discrepancy, looking for the answer—you will never get it; you only lead yourself on in the chase for your past.

Man seeks refuge from his worries; he cannot seek refuge from himself. In this, he pleads with reality, trying to attach himself to external things.

He waits, hoping one will find him—no one comes.

He sleeps, though even in sleep his mind refuses him peace. The world he fled returns in another form - the commander stands before judgement, but whose judgement is it? His enemies’, God’s, or merely that of his own conscience?

Looking above, the blade so imposing—is this the end? I close my eyes and wake up. The fables of my mind have run rampant again. I open my eyes: no blade, no crowd of haughty onlookers—just silence, the reflective examination of isolation. Have I passed this trial? Or has the nightmare of hell just begun?

He leaves the cave, encountering a monk by the river, a man who appears to possess that which the commander seeks. Yet he cannot determine what it is - wisdom, humility, or merely the absence of those passions which have enslaved him?

The monk lives by the river. Laypeople approach him: “So humble you are, oh monk.” Instinctively, the laypeople know that they lack what the monk has. They recognise something in another without having it in themselves—we all possess parts of the One, though to different extents; we all emit from the One.

All things happen in providence; the Logos binds even the strongest-willed men. We have our plans, yet Providence has His.

He spends his days ruled by destiny—or does providence not bind him?

Remember: what you call wisdom is nothing before God.

God is the chisel, I am the stone. Inwardly He carves me; outwardly I carve myself.

Hard times give opportunities to become principled and examine yourself even more so than good times.

Better to be a suffering servant than a successful slave.

Patience is a virtue, a virtue of prudence, one that, when followed, enables swiftness and self-obedience.

It is not what I do, but what you will do. One cannot lead the blind, but the blind must open his own eyes.

Reality represents itself; our feelings attempt to extrapolate it.

How can we retract ourselves from this world of feeling and emotion? Are we not a symphony of feeling and emotion? Would that be to separate from ourselves? But if we do not separate, are we attached? Do not fall into false dichotomies.

To know when you are emotional, you must have something non-emotional to attach yourself to—can you only know one thing in the absence of another?

We want solace in finality rather than the twisted temptations of uncertainty.

Aphorisms, proverbs, tall tales—how easy they are to proclaim, how tenuous they are to acclaim.

The man departs the river, carrying the same body, the same mind, yet with another question - has he attained wisdom, or merely acquired new words with which to explain his failure? The monk returns to his solitude, the commander to his duties, though only one appears content with what he possesses.

It appears you write only when you are transitioning or need to—make it subconscious to reflect daily.

You tell yourself you will do something; you even admit you should not do it. Then you forget what you said and do something else.

After he is fed and has been given two days of meagre food, he betrays his discipline and returns to the pen, selling himself short. Happy with his unseen shortcoming, he smiles as he enters the embrace of the pigpen.

Straying from the tracks of God, I claim to miss the train, but only missed the mark, missed myself; therefore, missed You, God.

Be mindful of yourself; watch yourself. Are you only looking to God when you are weak? Do you forget Him when victory is granted? Do you run through the gates of the city and forget to look back at who sent you?

Don’t get caught up in your own reflections—you depend on God.

You are hungry, you are restless—go pray, face the east.

Life feels most dear alone; you notice more, and indeed must—as soon as you associate with others, their plebeian noise interferes with your thoughts.

Better to be alone and sharp than surrounded and dull.

The commander remembers his former army, the banners, the conquests, the victories - all now relics of a world he cannot return to. He seeks restoration, yet each attempt begins with contemplation and ends in the same place. Can one command an army from within a cave?

He has waited for this day, the day he would finally regain his inspiration.

You sit there and waste your day.

Your competitors are not.

Do it now, return to victory.

You wake up and instantly think of how to look impressive to others. This is wrong—correct yourself.

You exaggerate your life since you have not built anything noteworthy in it—conquer and attain treasure; perhaps with the spoils of war you could speak.

Walk in: the first and only thing—think of your task. Only gaze at what will benefit you; ignore all that will not.

How foolish it is to spend your last reserves. Don’t you know you’ll need them when the time comes?

When you enter a new environment, be wary. You may think new faces thus mean a new life and hence greater social interaction—don’t fool yourself. Nothing is new under the sun; if you yourself have not changed, your surroundings will not. Most people do not change themselves in new environments; they merely reveal different parts of their character.

Hiding under the crevice of false duty presses the issue forward but not away.

Moments are temporary and fleeting; avoidance lasts longer.

Do not wait until the armies have assembled on the field; your conscience knows when the march has begun—run to the fortress, return to proverbs of old, retract from conflict, make sure it never happens.

The devil throws all tricks at you; he begs for your destruction—do not let foul words with a liar bring you back to despair.

Don’t let the crows peck at your remains; if necessary, let them fly behind you, willingly use them in battle.

Peace, peace—how easily the word is spoken. But am I to give up all that I possess within myself?

Running makes the truth slip further from you; accepting reveals what will always be revealed.

He stands before the entrance, looking upon the world which he abandoned. The mind tells him to return, the body remains still - perhaps the armies of his conscience have not yet reconciled themselves. How strange it is, a commander who once feared no mortal now hesitates before the ordinary affairs of life.

Damaged, scarred, fractured—can you ever repair, or can you merely cover up the past?

Am I the victor, or have I merely held out the longest?

What force could redeem such a man and allow him to exit the cave—surely not himself?

Alas, the commander stands between two kingdoms, one he has lost and another he has imagined - neither offering him the certainty he so desperately seeks. Will providence raise him from his ruins, or has he mistaken another moment of inspiration for the restoration of himself? He looks towards the world, though whether he shall march forward or retreat once more, even he cannot know.

title: Three Assorted Poems
excerpt: Reader, imagine a man—his mind a fortress, his heart a captive to the passions he so desperately attempts to govern.
body:
Reader, imagine a man—his mind a fortress, his heart a captive to the passions he so desperately attempts to govern. He sits alone, pondering the past, the present, and that which may never come to pass.

The Archangel Gabriel appears before him, bestowing upon the man three poems. He looks upon them, recognising in each a part of himself—one of love departed, another of love restrained, and the last of love imagined.

Could this be a gift of consolation, or merely another trial of the passions? Has providence granted him wisdom, or has the man been given another means to enslave himself to his own delusions?

He cannot know. Alas, what he once sought to command has now become his master. He takes up his pen, for the words of the mind are more comfortable than the words of the physical.

I. Her

Years after your passing, melancholy reigns tyrannically.

Somber he who is alive; appeased is she who is no more.

In the world you left behind, the living envy the dead.

My will to love you is here; your will to resurrect is not.

Defiled in life you were; in death, sanctified you are.

Your piano still plays, each note a reminder.

Your smile still shines, each memory an indicator.

Long nights with you, longer eternity without you.

II. Under This Sun

Thinking about you, under this sun—however hot and dusty it is.

The rays beam down onto me, beating me dark.

However, what beats me more is you not being here—sitting at this table alone—your smile and warmth, vacant.

However, such is life. As the sun retires each day, my mind does not retire from you, for without need for sword nor stick, you appear to have captured my mind.

Rendered me a hostage, a prisoner of my own delusions—I do not dare to cast the dice, to play with fortune, to ask you back into my life.

For I know my obligation: keep you at arm’s length, for I know honour comes before dismay—dismay at my delusions being just what they are.

III. Your Smile Still Glows

Your smile still glows, teeth white—lips plump, and your beautiful skin, caramel—just like mine—a delight for only the most knowledgeable.

For you are rare, one not found so easily. I know losing you would be to lose more—to lose hope, perhaps.

Could it be you have become an idol, a person who I made an image of—just that, an image, something still and never a showing of the present reality?

My stoicism persists, not allowing you to attain me—though not physically, you shall not attain my mind.

The mind wanders on, wishing you thought about it too—we all know the reality.

I can’t help but concoct your smile—I cannot help but to concoct a plan, a plan to win you over. Oh, how the old general was silenced by the sword.

Poetry, my only way to communicate with you.

Look at the stars, I ask… where is mine?

The man lays down his pen, pondering the message bestowed upon him by Gabriel. Is this consolation from the heavens, or merely another affliction of the earthly passions? The angel has departed, yet the words remain—each a reminder of that which he possesses no longer, that which he desires, and that which may never be.

Could providence have sent consolation in the form of suffering? Or has the man, in his perpetual pursuit of meaning, mistaken the chains of his own desires for gifts from the heavens?

Alas, the messenger has spoken, yet the man remains without an answer. Is it Gabriel’s message he fails to understand, or is it himself?

title: Why do men look up to UFC fighters?
excerpt: What is it about observing a man knock someone out, just as he predicted, that lights a flame within us?
body:
What is it about observing a man knock someone out, just as he predicted, that lights a flame within us?

Could it be that glory, fame, and domination justify the pride we have in ourselves—that which is already present, waiting to be displayed for the world to see? An escape route for the inner workings of our ego, released through the adrenaline of a knockout. All of us must desire this release; few of us ever get the chance.

Victory seems to justify pride. When God denies it, is it really a defeat, or merely a lesson?

title: Friends from Orbit?
excerpt: Why do women have the natural ability to spot the group leader?
body:
Why do women have the natural ability to spot the group leader? That single man just seems to pull all other men within his radius towards him. The sun: a blazing inferno, though also the guiding light the galaxy cannot survive without. Larger friends, whether in personality, physical size, or knowledge, seem to pull those close to them into their orbit.

In the same way, a weaker country often becomes the vassal of a larger neighbouring state. Over time, it slowly loses its own unique customs, traditions, and culture, eventually becoming a memory of the past. Men, like countries, appear to rise and fall. When in decline, they tend to orbit around those still burning with the passion of naïve youth and eventually implode.

title: How Can Smart People "Fall For" Religion or the Right?
excerpt: The idea that being religious or right-wing is somehow tied to being unintelligent or ignorant is a relatively new development — largely a product of the past 30 years.
body:
The idea that being religious or right-wing is somehow tied to being unintelligent or ignorant is a relatively new development — largely a product of the past 30 years. It is not a historical norm, and it certainly is not an intellectual truth.

For the majority of human history, many of the smartest people were deeply religious and, by extension, socially conservative. Religion was not seen as the enemy of reason, but as the framework through which reason operated. Philosophy, ethics, law, science, and governance were all shaped within religious worldviews, not in opposition to them.

Many of the universities that modern progressives now pride themselves on attending were founded by Christians. These institutions were originally built on the assumption that truth, morality, and reason were interconnected. Even many of the values progressives hold dear today — empathy, compassion, kindness, charity, and respect for human dignity — were propagated and systematised by Christianity long before they were secularised.

Yet this historical lineage is often forgotten. There is a widespread assumption that modern society emerged despite religion rather than through it. As a result, religious belief is frequently dismissed as a primitive holdover, and conservatism is framed as resistance to progress rather than as a form of historical memory.

What is rarely confronted is the alternative. When religion is not simply replaced with pluralism or humility, but aggressively removed and substituted with ideology, the results can be catastrophic. Truly secular states that attempted to erase religion entirely — such as the Soviet Union or Communist China — did not produce utopias of reason and compassion. They produced some of the worst atrocities of the modern era, justified not by God, but by the state, the party, or "historical necessity."

This does not mean that atheism itself causes violence, nor that religion is immune to abuse. It means that human beings do not stop believing when religion disappears — they simply redirect belief elsewhere. When transcendent moral limits are removed, power fills the vacuum.

Smart people do not "fall for" religion or conservatism. Many arrive at them through reflection, history, and scepticism of ideological certainty. Conservatism, at its core, is not about rejecting change, but about questioning whether new ideas improve on institutions that evolved for reasons often forgotten.

The modern habit of equating intelligence with secular progressivism is less a mark of insight than of cultural conformity. It flatters those who hold it, but it explains very little about history, human nature, or the foundations of the society we currently inhabit.

Intelligence alone does not guarantee wisdom. Without humility, historical awareness, and moral restraint, it often produces nothing more than confidence without limits — and history has shown where that can lead.

title: The Relationship Crisis No One Wants to Talk About
excerpt: From the perspective of someone under 25, modern relationships increasingly feel transactional, shallow, and insecure.
body:
From the perspective of someone under 25, modern relationships increasingly feel transactional, shallow, and insecure. Dating no longer seems rooted in trust, shared purpose, or long-term commitment, but instead in appearance, convenience, and social validation. Relationships are often less about genuine connection and more about how they look online — who you’re seen with, what you post together, and how desirable that makes you appear to others.

Social media and dating apps have fundamentally changed the dynamic. At any moment, your partner may have dozens of alternative options sitting in their pocket. This constant availability of replacements undermines security and discourages emotional investment. Why commit deeply when everything feels provisional?

Many young men feel particularly frustrated by the modern dating landscape. Third-wave feminism, in their view, has promoted high expectations from men while rejecting traditional reciprocal roles such as cooperation, support, or complementarity. Instead, career advancement and individualism are prioritised, often leaving relationships feeling one-sided or conditional.

This has created a distorted dating market, especially among Generation Z. A small group of highly successful, wealthy, or high-status men tend to attract a disproportionate share of female attention, while a large number of other men are left excluded entirely. These men are often labelled “incels,” but in reality many are simply disengaged, discouraged, or opting out altogether. Interestingly, even the men who succeed most in this system often report dissatisfaction. They describe partners as over-demanding, emotionally volatile, and shaped by extensive prior relationships that make genuine bonding difficult.

At the same time, there is a growing sense of fear among men. Dating now carries not only emotional risk, but reputational and legal anxiety. The idea that a single accusation — true or false — could permanently damage one’s life has made many men cautious, withdrawn, and hesitant to pursue relationships at all.

Women, however, are far from happy in this environment either.

Many express frustration that men appear weak, passive, or unwilling to initiate. Masculinity feels diluted. Men often lack direction, confidence, or a clear path in life. This is not simply a personal failure, but a generational one. Many young men grew up without strong father figures and were shaped more by online culture than by real-world male role models. The result is uncertainty about how to act, lead, or commit.

What emerges is a mutual resentment. Men feel rejected, disposable, and undervalued. Women feel disappointed, unsupported, and unimpressed. Each side blames the other, while the underlying structures that created this situation go largely unexamined.

The result is a genuine relationship crisis.

The divide between young men and women has reached an all-time high — socially, politically, and economically. Trust is eroding. Shared expectations are disappearing. Intimacy is increasingly commodified, and long-term commitment feels risky rather than rewarding.

This is not simply a cultural mood swing. It is a systemic breakdown driven by technology, economic pressure, ideological confusion, and the collapse of shared pathways into adulthood. Yet it remains one of the least openly discussed crises of our time.

Until society confronts these issues honestly — without reflexive blame or ideological defensiveness — the alienation between the sexes will continue to deepen. And the longer it goes unaddressed, the harder it will be to repair.

title: Relationships in the 2020s: Really a Platonic Form of Beauty?
excerpt: Plato, one of the great saints of Western philosophy, lived almost 2,500 years ago.
body:
Plato, one of the great saints of Western philosophy, lived almost 2,500 years ago. His words, through his own works or through writing down the words of his teacher, Socrates, still influence many to this day and continue to enlighten others on the beauty of classical philosophy. Among the many things Plato discussed in his time—mainly, what virtue is and whether it can be taught, the ideal government structure, how leaders should function, or how we understand the metaphysical realm—one sticks out to me the most. My first introduction to this concept was in Plato’s Socratic dialogue, the Phaedo, where, among the many things discussed, I first heard about the concept of Forms as Plato describes it.

Beauty, apparent in some things to some and apparent in other things to others—can its true nature be pinpointed? And if it can be, then what exactly is it, to be precise? These are among a few of the questions raised in the Phaedo. Although we recognise beauty through many different things, Plato’s idea suggests that these beautiful things may share in something higher and more perfect than themselves. We find many things beautiful, and those things are often different for different people, yet they may still direct us towards a greater Form of Beauty.

How does this tie into relationships, though? So far, we have discussed only, in a very basic sense, the ideas surrounding Platonic Forms. My proposition is quite simple: as it concerns the Form of Beauty, relationships, for the majority of history, have been seen as something which may participate in or guide us towards it—something which, for the majority of the history of mankind, has enticed us, been the stage of tragedy and hope, helped us understand ourselves, and allowed us to experience parts of ourselves we never knew before.

Although, if one has been paying attention, one would realise that I said “the majority” of history. That is to say, there is something about modern relationships which actually leads people to have an aversion to them as they are currently portrayed in social life and popular media—something which dilutes the beauty found within relationships and leads people to view them with antipathy.

What has caused the average person to experience a heinous erosion in his love for relationships? Is it feminism? Is it the economy? Is it the crisis of morality? Throughout the Western world, since the 1970s, there has been a large uptick in divorces, remarriages, and people who remain single without children. Among the youth of Generation Z, many feel a quiet resentment towards the era’s culture: one-night hookups, sneaky links, situationships, unfaithful relationships, and relationships ending explosively.

Is it a coincidence that the generation—Generation Z—which follows Generation X, who normalised divorced parents, broken homes, and separated families, subsequently has the highest rates of loneliness and feelings of having no meaning in life? Could these two be contingent on one another?

These are merely thoughts on the era of history in which many find themselves: the 2020s. Some say this is merely a repeat of the fall of any civilisation, nothing new in history. Others say it is the eerie death creak of a world which no longer exists. Furthermore, what that entails is that this is how it will always be from now on: relationships forever being discarded as something no longer to be heralded as beautiful, no longer something capable of guiding us towards the Form of Beauty. Plato would be turning in his grave.
